title: Fresnel's Biprism
short_intro: Fresnel's biprism is an optical device used to produce sustained interference fringes from a single monochromatic source by division of wavefront. It consists of two prisms of very small refracting angles placed base-to-base to form a single isosceles prism.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the construction of the biprism, virtual source separation, fringe width formula, and measurement of wavelength of light.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of virtual source distance, angular fringe width, effect of inserting a thin transparent film in the path of one of the interfering beams, and white light fringe patterns.

prerequisites: Refraction through a Prism of Small Angle

concept_notes.heading: Construction and Working Principle
bullets: A Fresnel biprism is constructed from a single plate of glass ground and polished so that its two adjacent refracting surfaces inclined at a very small angle (typically around 0.5 degrees) meet to form an obtuse angle of nearly 179 degrees.
When a monochromatic slit source is placed symmetrically in front of the obtuse angle, the upper half of the biprism acts as a prism bending light downwards, and the lower half bends light upwards.
The emergent wavefronts appear to diverge from two coherent virtual sources formed behind the biprism, satisfying the requirement for division of wavefront interference.

concept_notes.heading: Formation of Interference Fringes
bullets: The two virtual sources S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> act as coherent sources because they originate from the same primary source S.
In the region where the two emergent beams overlap on a screen placed at a distance from the biprism, alternative dark and bright interference bands are formed.
The central fringe is always bright because the waves reaching the center from both virtual sources travel equal optical paths, resulting in zero phase difference.

concept_notes.heading: Measurement of Wavelength and Source Separation
bullets: The fringe width β is given by β = λD / d, where λ is the wavelength of light, D is the distance between the source and the screen, and d is the distance between the two virtual sources.

Direct measurement of the separation d between virtual sources is difficult because S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are virtual; hence, a convex lens is used to form real images of the virtual sources on a micrometer eyepiece.

Using the displacement method with a convex lens, d is determined using the relation d = sqrt(d<sub>1</sub>d<sub>2</sub>), where d<sub>1</sub> and d<sub>2</sub> are the image separations in two conjugate positions of the lens.

concept_notes.heading: Effect of Thin Film in the Path of Interference
bullets: When a transparent thin film of refractive index μ and thickness t is introduced in the path of one of the interfering beams, the entire fringe system gets shifted towards the side of the film.
The lateral shift of the fringes is given by x = (μ - 1)t D / d.
By measuring the fringe shift, either the thickness of the film or its refractive index can be precisely determined.

derivations.title: Derivation of Fringe Width β
derivations.conditions: Monochromatic light of wavelength λ, distance between source and screen = D, separation between virtual sources = d.
steps: Let S be the slit source and S<sub>1</sub>, S<sub>2</sub> be the virtual sources separated by distance d.
Let a be the distance from source S to the biprism, and b be the distance from the biprism to the screen. Then total distance D = a + b.

Consider a point P on the screen at a distance x from the central maximum O. The path difference Δ between the two interfering waves arriving at P from S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> is Δ = S<sub>2</sub>P - S<sub>1</sub>P.
Using geometric approximation for S<sub>2</sub>P<sup>2</sup> - S<sub>1</sub>P<sup>2</sup>, the path difference evaluates to Δ ≈ xd / D.
For constructive interference (bright fringe), Δ = nλ, giving x<sub>n</sub> = nλD / d.
For destructive interference (dark fringe), Δ = (n + 1/2)λ, giving x<sub>n</sub> = (n + 1/2)λD / d.
The fringe width β is the distance between two consecutive bright or dark fringes: β = x<sub>n+1</sub> - x<sub>n</sub>.

derivations.title: Derivation of Separation d Between Virtual Sources
derivations.conditions: Biprism of refractive index μ and small refracting angle α.
steps: A ray from source S at distance a from the biprism strikes the upper face at angle of incidence nearly equal to zero.
The deviation δ produced by a thin prism of small angle α and refractive index μ is given by δ = (μ - 1)α.
The two virtual sources S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are formed at distance a from the source (or a + b from the biprism depending on convention, here taken at distance a from S).
The angle subtended by S<sub>1</sub>S<sub>2</sub> at the biprism is 2δ.
Therefore, the separation between the virtual sources is d = 2 a δ = 2 a (μ - 1)α.

formula_sheet.name: Fringe Width
formula_sheet.variables: β = fringe width, λ = wavelength, D = distance from source to screen, d = separation between virtual sources
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for small angles and monochromatic light

formula_sheet.name: Virtual Source Separation
formula_sheet.variables: a = distance from slit to biprism, μ = refractive index of glass, α = refracting angle of biprism

formula_sheet.name: Lens Method for Source Separation
formula_sheet.variables: d<sub>1</sub> = image separation in first conjugate position, d<sub>2</sub> = image separation in second conjugate position
formula_sheet.conditions: Convex lens placed between biprism and screen

formula_sheet.name: Fringe Shift due to Thin Film
formula_sheet.variables: t = thickness of thin film, μ = refractive index of film
formula_sheet.conditions: Film placed normal to one interfering beam

formula_sheet.name: Path Difference
formula_sheet.variables: x = distance from central maximum on screen

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fresnel's Biprism Experimental Arrangement
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An optical bench layout showing sodium lamp, narrow vertical slit S, Fresnel's biprism, convex lens for measuring d, and micrometer eyepiece on the optical bench rail.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the physical alignment of components required to observe interference fringes by division of wavefront.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in viva voce and conceptual matching questions regarding bench alignment.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity Distribution of Interference Fringes
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of Light Intensity (I) on the y-axis versus Position on Screen (x) on the x-axis, showing uniform periodic maxima and minima with equal spacing β.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that interference fringes have equal width and equal intensity across the pattern, unlike diffraction patterns.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing interference patterns from diffraction patterns in multiple-choice questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Conjugate Focus Method for d Measurement
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A ray diagram showing two positions of a convex lens forming magnified (d<sub>1</sub>) and diminished (d<sub>2</sub>) real images of virtual sources S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> in an eyepiece.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves that the source separation can be accurately calculated as the geometric mean of two image sizes using the principle of reversibility.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problem formulation and conceptual understanding of optical magnification.

solved_numericals.question: In a Fresnel's biprism experiment, the distance between the virtual sources is 0.6 mm and the screen is placed 1.0 m away from the sources. If the wavelength of light used is 589 nm, calculate the fringe width.
solution_steps: Identify given values: d = 0.6 mm = 0.6 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m, D = 1.0 m, λ = 589 nm = 589 × 10<sup>-9</sup> m.
Write the formula for fringe width: β = (λD) / d.

solved_numericals.question: A Fresnel's biprism of refracting angle 1 degree and refractive index 1.5 is placed at a distance of 20 cm from a slit illuminated by light of wavelength 6000 Å. Find the fringe width on a screen placed 80 cm from the biprism.
solution_steps: Given: α = 1° = π / 180 radians, μ = 1.5, a = 20 cm = 0.2 m, b = 80 cm = 0.8 m, λ = 6000 Å = 6 × 10<sup>-7</sup> m.
Total distance from source to screen D = a + b = 0.2 + 0.8 = 1.0 m.
Calculate virtual source separation d = 2 a (μ - 1) α = 2 × 0.2 × (1.5 - 1) × (π / 180) = 0.4 × 0.5 × (3.1416 / 180) = 3.49 × 10<sup>-3</sup> m.

solved_numericals.question: When a mica sheet of refractive index 1.58 and thickness 6 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m is placed in the path of one of the interfering beams in a biprism setup, the fringes shift by a distance equal to 15 fringe widths. Find the wavelength of light used.
solution_steps: Given: μ = 1.58, t = 6 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m, shift x<sub>0</sub> = 15 β = 15 (λD / d).
Formula for fringe shift: x<sub>0</sub> = (μ - 1) t D / d.
Equating the two expressions: 15 (λD / d) = (μ - 1) t D / d.
Cancel D and d from both sides: 15 λ = (μ - 1) t.

assumptions_and_limitations: The refracting angle of the biprism is assumed to be very small, which validates the thin prism deviation formula δ = (μ - 1)α.
The source slit must be extremely narrow and parallel to the refracting edge of the biprism to ensure good fringe visibility and contrast.
The distance D from source to screen is much greater than the source separation d (D >> d), validating the approximations used in deriving the path difference.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Fresnel's biprism produces interference by division of amplitude.
common_misconceptions.correct: It produces interference by division of wavefront.
common_misconceptions.why: A single wavefront from the slit is split into two wavefronts by the two halves of the biprism, acting as two virtual sources.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The central fringe in a biprism interference pattern is dark.
common_misconceptions.correct: The central fringe is always bright.
common_misconceptions.why: The waves from virtual sources travel equal optical paths to reach the center of the screen, resulting in zero path difference and constructive interference.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Fringe width depends on the distance of the biprism from the source (a) and screen (b) individually.
common_misconceptions.correct: Fringe width depends only on the total distance D = a + b between the source and the screen.
common_misconceptions.why: Mathematically, β = λD / d, where D is the total distance from the primary source to the screen.

quick_revision: Fresnel's biprism uses division of wavefront to form two coherent virtual sources.
Virtual source separation is given by d = 2a(μ - 1)α.
Central fringe in biprism interference is always bright.
Introduction of a transparent film shifts the entire fringe pattern towards the film side without altering fringe width.
